quiz.explanation: ICE = Impact (how much will it move the needle?) × Confidence (how sure are we?) × Ease (how quickly can we ship?). The highest-scoring items get built first.

lessons.title: From MVP to Product-Market Fit
lessons.subtitle: PMF isn't a moment — it's a feeling confirmed by data. Understand the signals, the metrics, and the mindset shift.

cards.headline: Superhuman's 40% Rule
cards.body: Rahul Vohra, founder of Superhuman (a $33/mo email app), needed a way to measure product-market fit. He used Sean Ellis's now-famous question: "How would you feel if you could no longer use this product?" If 40% or more say "very disappointed," you have PMF. When Superhuman first measured this, they were at 33%. Not there yet. So Vohra segmented: which TYPES of users said "very disappointed"? He doubled down on serving those people brilliantly and ignored the rest. Within months, they crossed 40%. The lesson: PMF isn't about making everyone happy. It's about making the RIGHT people ecstatic.

cards.headline: The Signals of Product-Market Fit
cards.body: Marc Andreessen says: "You can always feel when PMF is happening." But feelings need data to confirm them:
bullets: Users complain when it's down — they've built it into their workflow
Word-of-mouth growth — new users arrive without you spending on marketing
Usage grows faster than you can support — you're scrambling to keep up
Retention curves flatten — people stop leaving after a certain point

cards.headline: The PMF Metrics
cards.body: Quantitative signals that indicate you're approaching or have achieved PMF:
bullets: Sean Ellis test: 40%+ say "very disappointed" if the product disappeared
Day 30 retention above 20% (consumer) or 40% (SaaS)
NPS above 50 — users actively recommend you
Organic/referral traffic exceeds paid acquisition
cards.statLabel: "very disappointed" threshold — the quantitative benchmark for product-market fit

cards.headline: Pre-PMF vs. Post-PMF Mindset
cards.body: The biggest mistake founders make is optimising for growth before they have PMF. Before PMF: iterate on product, talk to users daily, measure retention, ignore vanity metrics. After PMF: invest in growth, build the team, raise money, scale operations. Premature scaling is the #1 cause of startup death (according to Startup Genome). Don't hire, don't spend on ads, don't expand to new markets until retention proves people need what you've built.

cards.headline: Your Day 20 Action
cards.body:
Run the Sean Ellis test on your current users. Send this one-question survey to everyone who's used your product at least twice:

"How would you feel if you could no longer use [product name]?"
- Very disappointed
- Somewhat disappointed
- Not disappointed

If you're above 40% "very disappointed" — congratulations, focus on growth. If you're below: segment the results. Who ARE the "very disappointed" people? What do they have in common? Double down on serving them better. Ignore everyone else for now.

quiz.question: What is the "40% rule" for measuring product-market fit?
options: If 40%+ of users say they'd be "very disappointed" without your product, you have PMF
If 40% of your revenue comes from repeat customers
If 40% of visitors convert to paying users
If you retain 40% of users after 12 months
quiz.explanation: Sean Ellis's test: ask users "How would you feel if you could no longer use this product?" If 40%+ say "very disappointed," you've achieved product-market fit.

quiz.question: What did Superhuman do when they measured below 40%?
options: Segmented users to find WHO was "very disappointed" and doubled down on serving them
Added more features to make everyone happy
Lowered their price to attract more users
Pivoted to a completely different product idea
quiz.explanation: Vohra segmented: which user types said "very disappointed"? He focused exclusively on making those people ecstatic — ignoring users who were lukewarm. This raised the score above 40%.

quiz.question: According to Startup Genome, what is the #1 cause of startup death?
options: Premature scaling — investing in growth before achieving product-market fit
Running out of funding before launch
Co-founder conflicts and team breakdowns
Being outcompeted by larger companies
quiz.explanation: Premature scaling — hiring, spending on ads, expanding markets before PMF — is the top killer. Growth without retention is a leaky bucket. Fix the product first, then scale.

lessons.title: Your 90-Day Post-MVP Roadmap
lessons.subtitle: You've validated your idea. Now what? Plan the next 90 days: what to build, who to hire, and how to scale without breaking.

cards.headline: Airbnb's First 90 Days After Validation
cards.body: After validating demand with their air mattress MVP, Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia didn't immediately build a polished platform. Their next 90 days were ruthlessly focused: (1) Days 1-30: Personally onboard every new host with professional photography. (2) Days 31-60: Build ONLY the features hosts asked for most (calendar, messaging). (3) Days 61-90: Expand from New York to one more city — not ten. They resisted the urge to "go big" and instead went deep. The result: they built a foundation that could scale to millions, because it worked perfectly for hundreds first.

cards.headline: The 30-60-90 Framework
cards.body: Structure your post-MVP roadmap in three phases. Each builds on validated learning from the previous:
bullets: Days 1-30: DEEPEN — Make your best users ecstatic. Fix the #1 pain point. Nail onboarding.
Days 31-60: EXPAND — Add the one feature users scream for. Start systematising what you do manually.
Days 61-90: SCALE — Move from manual to automated. Begin repeatable acquisition. Set up metrics dashboards.

cards.headline: What to Build vs. What to Hire
cards.body: In the first 90 days post-validation, your build priorities should focus on removing yourself as a bottleneck:
bullets: Build: Automated onboarding (replaces you manually welcoming each user)
Build: Self-serve support (FAQ, in-app guidance — replaces you answering every question)
Hire: Only if you physically cannot do the work yourself anymore
Outsource: Anything that's not your core value (design, bookkeeping, customer support)
cards.statLabel: days to go from validated MVP to scalable v1 — with focused execution

cards.headline: The "Scale Readiness" Checklist
cards.body: Before investing in growth, make sure your foundation is solid. You're ready to scale when: (1) Retention is stable or improving — people stay. (2) Unit economics work — you make more from a customer than it costs to acquire them. (3) Onboarding runs without you — new users succeed without hand-holding. (4) You can describe your ideal customer in one sentence — you know exactly who to target. If any of these are shaky, fix them first. Scaling a broken product just breaks it faster.

cards.headline: Your Day 21 Action
cards.body:
Write your personal 90-day post-MVP roadmap:

DAYS 1-30 (Deepen):
- The #1 thing I'll fix/improve: ___
- How I'll make my best users ecstatic: ___

DAYS 31-60 (Expand):
- The ONE feature I'll add (based on data): ___
- The ONE manual process I'll automate: ___

DAYS 61-90 (Scale):
- My repeatable acquisition channel: ___
- My "scale readiness" milestone: ___

Congratulations — you've completed the Build & Test Your MVP course. You now have a validated idea, a working product, and a plan for the next 90 days. Go build something people want.

quiz.question: What did Airbnb focus on in their first 30 days after validating the concept?
options: Personally onboarding every host with professional photography
Expanding to 10 cities simultaneously
Building a mobile app
Raising a Series A from venture capitalists
quiz.explanation: Chesky and Gebbia went DEEP, not wide. They personally onboarded each new host, provided professional photography, and made the experience perfect for a small group before expanding.

quiz.question: In the 30-60-90 framework, what is the focus of Days 31-60?
options: EXPAND — add the most-requested feature and start systematising manual processes
SCALE — invest heavily in paid marketing and automation
DEEPEN — continue making existing users ecstatic
PIVOT — evaluate whether to change direction entirely
quiz.explanation: Days 31-60 is the EXPAND phase: add the one feature users are screaming for, and begin turning manual processes into repeatable systems. Not yet scaling — just expanding capability.

quiz.question: What must be true before you invest in scaling growth?
options: Retention is stable, unit economics work, and onboarding runs without you
You have at least $1M in funding secured
You've been featured in major press outlets
Your product has 10,000+ registered users
quiz.explanation: Scale readiness requires: stable retention (people stay), positive unit economics (LTV > CAC), and self-serve onboarding (users succeed without you). Scaling without these just breaks things faster.
